title: Railroads of the Raj: Estimating the Impact of Transportation Infrastructure
synthesis: Numbered implications become an empirical sequence. Historical and data detail earn their place by identifying variation or explaining a mechanism. Fit, identification, and counterfactual credibility remain distinct.

title: Railroads and American Economic Growth: A Market Access Approach
synthesis: The historical counterfactual motivates market access. Data construction, equilibrium closure, and robustness are explained as choices that change the economic interpretation, not merely implementation details.

title: Nonparametric Counterfactual Predictions in Neoclassical Models of International Trade
synthesis: The exposition moves through general economic representation, counterfactual recovery, identification, and finite-data implementation. Additional operational restrictions are named when introduced rather than attributed to the initial general theory.

title: Putting Quantitative Models to the Test: An Application to the U.S.-China Trade War
synthesis: Model validation is organized around a particular causal answer. The paper distinguishes raw fit, instrument-based evidence, power, and mechanical agreement with estimation moments.

title: Blending Theory and Data: A Space Odyssey
synthesis: Examples explain how theory connects observed outcomes to the desired counterfactual. The valuation argument remains separate from the identification of its inputs. The review essay's metaphors are useful pedagogically, not a template for every research introduction.

title: Imports, Exports, and Earnings Inequality: Measures of Exposure and Estimates of Incidence
version: Published QJE article, 2022; PDF begins at journal page 1553
synthesis: General factor-demand reasoning comes before operational CES restrictions. Exposure measures motivate, but do not replace, incidence estimation. Robustness distinguishes changes in distributional shape from changes in magnitude.

title: Trade and the Topography of the Spatial Economy
synthesis: The economic and geographic components are presented separately, then combined. Simple geometries explain equilibrium forces before real-world recovery. Spatial decomposition and infrastructure exercises have distinct purposes.

title: Universal Gravity
synthesis: A common representation links model properties, propagation, estimation, and a counterfactual. The exposition explains both what the class includes and what its restrictions exclude.

title: The Welfare Effects of Transportation Infrastructure Improvements
synthesis: Routing, traffic, congestion, and location choice form a feedback argument. Two models are developed in parallel, consolidated, and then connected to empirical tools. Measurement shortcuts accompany predictive comparisons.

title: Economic Activity across Space: A Supply and Demand Approach
version: Published JEP article, 2023; bundle pages 21-46 only
synthesis: Local supply and demand establish intuition before global linkages. Diagrams carry adjustment steps, while the data discussion explains implementation pitfalls. The essay is a pedagogical reference rather than a universal mathematical format.

title: Information Frictions in Trade
version: Published Econometrica article, 2014; permission cover excluded
synthesis: Empirical regularities motivate a search mechanism; the model then returns to those same regularities. Predictive evaluation uses an explicitly separate period. Extensive and intensive margins are not collapsed into one fit statistic.

title: Persistence and Path Dependence: A Primer
synthesis: Persistence, equilibrium uniqueness, and path dependence are distinguished early. Economic interpretations follow the dynamic equations, while simpler and extended models retain explicit boundaries.

title: New Trade Models, Same Old Gains?
synthesis: A simple model explains the welfare formula before the general result. Primitive assumptions, aggregate restrictions, ex-post valuation, and ex-ante prediction are separated. Empirical implementation is not presumed model-free.

title: Market Penetration Costs and the New Consumers Margin in International Trade
synthesis: A concrete mismatch in exporter behavior motivates consumer-reaching costs. Qualitative implications, empirical patterns, calibration, and counterfactuals remain separate stages. Aggregate agreement can coexist with distinct micro predictions.

title: A Unified Theory of Firm Selection and Growth
synthesis: Firm entry, selection, growth, and aggregate implications are connected through explicit objects. Calibration and prediction are separated. Simulation notes explain how model and data samples are made comparable.

title: The Elusive Pro-Competitive Effects of Trade
synthesis: Opposing markup mechanisms motivate a welfare question. Macroeconomic equivalence does not imply welfare equivalence. Competing empirical estimates, finite changes, and modeling limits receive distinct treatment.

title: The Economics of Density: Evidence from the Berlin Wall
version: Published Econometrica article, 2015; permission cover excluded
synthesis: The historical episode supplies identifying variation rather than scenery. Exogenous-characteristic recovery is distinguished from estimation of endogenous externalities. Reduced-form reorientation, structural parameters, and counterfactual predictions occupy separate evidentiary stages.

title: The Making of the Modern Metropolis: Evidence from London
synthesis: A workplace-residence mechanism links history, reduced-form evidence, recursive recovery, and counterfactuals. More restrictive structural exercises enter later, with their extra assumptions stated. Absolute and proportional spatial changes are carefully distinguished.

title: Commuting, Migration and Local Employment Elasticities
synthesis: Commuting links explain heterogeneous local employment responses. The paper carries residence/workplace distinctions through theory, measurement, simulated shocks, and independent evidence. Geographic aggregation does not silently eliminate cross-boundary links.

title: Measuring Aggregate Price Indexes with Taste Shocks: Theory and Evidence for CES Preferences
version: Published QJE article, 2020; PDF title uses Indices
synthesis: The price-index argument distinguishes residual interpretations, normalization, inversion, and aggregation. Empirical comparisons isolate alternative sources of disagreement instead of changing several assumptions at once.

title: Quantitative Spatial Economics
synthesis: A taxonomy of spatial ingredients precedes concrete models. Closure, ownership, spatial support, inversion, and multiplicity are treated as economic choices. Numerical illustrations remain explicitly stylized.

title: Quantitative Urban Models: From Theory to Data
synthesis: Concrete within-city patterns motivate an accessible model. Worker and firm choices carry the explanation with limited notation. Model variants are selected for the question and available data rather than presented as an automatic realism ladder.

title: The Economics of Spatial Mobility: Theory and Evidence Using Smartphone Data
synthesis: The itinerary is defined early and linked to complementarity and substitution. The empirical object, computational solution, and equilibrium extension are separate contributions. Model/data comparisons label normalized quantities and scenario restrictions.
